title: Lesson 3 - Choosing and Scheduling the Learning Rate
author: Sample course (bundled with the project)

segments.text: this lesson is entirely about the learning rate, which we have mentioned twice and kept postponing. the learning rate decides
how far you move along the negative gradient on each step. if it is too small, training crawls and you
run out of patience or compute budget before the loss comes down. if it is too large, you overshoot the
valley, bounce from wall to wall, and the loss diverges to infinity. you will see that in your logs as
nan values appearing. so how do you pick one. the practical answer is a learning rate range test. you start
with a very small rate, increase it steadily over a few hundred iterations, and plot the loss against the rate.
the best choice is usually just below the point where the loss starts climbing. after that, use a schedule. it
is common to start relatively large and decay over training, because early on you want to cover ground quickly and
later you want to settle into the bottom of the valley rather than bouncing around it. cosine decay and step
decay are both fine, and the specific schedule matters far less than having one at all. finally, the optimisers. momentum
keeps a running average of past gradients so you build speed in consistent directions and damp oscillation across a narrow
valley. rmsprop scales the step per parameter so rarely updated parameters still move. adam combines both, which is why it
is the default in most codebases. it is not always the best, but it is almost never terrible, and that
is a good property for a default. that is the end of the course.
